translation:
It was the abode (nivas-sthan) of the Supreme, and therefore the Supreme is called Narayan.

_tasminnande sa bhagavanushitva parivatsaram || svayamevatmano dhyanattadandamakarod dvidha ||8||_ (Manusmriti 1-2) (In that egg, that Lord dwelt for one year during the earlier time of dissolution, and then, by his own self-contemplation, he divided it into two parts.)

Kabirji goes on to say that among the eighty-four lakh living souls, male and female were also created — these are known as human beings. (_ek narke ang pahechan_ — recognise the mark of the one Being) — that is, if a human being simply recognizes maya, the Lord who dwells eternally in the cosmic egg says, "I come eternally into the womb-contemplation." Parbrahm is attained naturally and effortlessly. In all eighty-four lakh species alike, sexual desire develops in the same way in male and female; in the conception of all eighty-four lakh species, sexual desire develops naturally in this same manner.

So Shri Vasudev spoke thus, to the gods: "Whatever doubts and misgivings are in your minds, let me remove them." Parbrahm, taking the form of the Hansa (swan) avatar, separated milk and water into their distinct portions (the "nimedo"). In this universe there are two paths — the path of action (karma-marg) and the path of non-action (nishkarma-marg) — and their mixing has created confusion; he resolved this confused mixture of doubt. Twenty-four avatars have been enumerated, among which the Hansa avatar was taken for this very purpose. Therefore those on the path of action have described four things as the gateway to attaining the first liberation. Their names are:

1. Salokya: After death, the soul can dwell together with the Supreme, Parbrahm.

2. Sarupya: After death, the soul takes on a form just like Parbrahm's and dwells with the Supreme.

3. Sanidhya: After death, the soul, retaining its own original identity and individuality, dwells with Parbrahm as a special personal companion, with that status.

4. Sayujya: After death, the soul merges completely into oneness with the Supreme, becoming one essence with Him — becoming unified, dissolved in the feeling of oneness.

Regarding the four liberations, Jivanji Maharaj says:

_char mugat mide bhai, jahan prem bhakti prakash || jivanmukt jan jivana, jahan sadguru shabda vishvas ||29||_ (Sadguru Jivandasji Maharaj says that the four kinds of liberation — sayujya, samipya, sarupya, salokya — count for nothing wherever the light of the tenth kind of devotion, prema-lakshana bhakti, love-natured devotion, shines. One who has love-natured devotion is truly jivanmukta, liberated while living; one's jivanmukta state rests only in firm faith in the Sadguru's word.)

Vyasdasji says:

_vyas char mugat bilbat phire, shri vrindavanki khor, mohe bas kyun na vrajmein diyo, main nirakhun jugal kishor ||30||_ (Vyasdasji says that all four kinds of liberation wander about restlessly and bewildered in the narrow lanes of Vrindavan, saying, "Why did the Lord not grant us the privilege of dwelling in Vraj? We would have had the privilege of beholding Shri Krishna.")

It is written in Kalyan, Yoga special issue (Yogank), page 466:

_mukti kahat gopalso, meri mukti karay, vraj raj udi mastak chadhai, mukti mukt hvai jaay ||31||_ (Mukti, Liberation herself, implores Lord Krishna, saying, "Show me how I too may be liberated." The Lord replied, "If the dust of Vraj rises and settles upon your head, then even Liberation would be liberated.")

It is said in the Bhagavat:

_salokya-sarshti-sarupyaikatvamapyuta, diyamanam na grihnanti vina matsevanam janah ||9||_ (Skandha 3, Adhyaya 29, verse 13) (Loving devotees, without giving up service to the Lord, do not accept it even when the Lord offers them these five kinds of liberation — salokya, sarshti, samipya, sarupya, and sayujya, oneness. That is to say, before devotion, liberation is but a lowly servant fetching water.)

Salokya = dwelling in the same realm as the Lord.

Sarshti = attaining splendor equal to the Lord's.

Samipya = dwelling near the Lord.

Sarupya = attaining a four-armed form like the Lord's.

Ekatva, oneness = becoming one with the Lord, as the water of the Ganga becomes one with the ocean.

Among these, salokya liberation is given even to a great enemy such as Shishupal; therefore true devotees hold no desire for liberation. In Krishnadas's Parichari it is said of liberation:

_jaiso narak taisi mukti, jiv abujh jane nahi jukti ||_ (Liberation is just like hell; the ignorant soul does not understand this truth.) Jivanji Maharaj told Krishnadas that liberation is just like a jail, like hell.

In a certain sakhi, couplet, it is said:

_santsangat so janiye, jake dradh vrat hari naam, char mugat mange nahi, aur vaikunthko dham ||_ (From the company of saints one learns that those who hold firm faith in the Lord's name do not ask for the four liberations, nor do they ask even for the abode of Vaikunth.)

Narsinh Mehta sings — a Prabhatiyu (morning hymn):

_jire char mugatni jugat chhe jujvi murakh mati kari ek thare, bhagatne mugatno bhed rude dhare pativrat hari naam tahaan kavan saare, jire saharupi mugat sanmukh nirkhe hari samipi aasan paas aape, saharupi sahajoti mugat behu doholi bhaav vina bhagati hari kem thaaye, jire murate surat ghare kumat mat aachare avigatnath deva da deva, jahaan jahaan bhid pade nij bhagatne taanhaan pragat thai kare aap seva, gopinath garuva mune dheen jaani taahara dasna charanni paas rakhe, bhane narsaiyo hunto leen maya vishe dheen chhun dheen chhun em bhaakhe_ (The four kinds of liberation each follow a different way, but those of foolish understanding take devotion and liberation to be one and the same, keeping this confusion of devotion and liberation within their hearts — so how then can they attain single-minded devotion to the Lord's name? Through sanidhya liberation one may behold the Lord face to face, and through samipya liberation the Lord keeps one near him; but sarupya and sayujya liberation are both very bad indeed. So without the feeling of exclusive, loving devotion, how can true devotion arise? People fix their minds on the worship of images and thereby practice a corrupted understanding, but the Supreme, whose movement none can grasp, is the God of gods. Wherever his own devotee suffers pain and distress, there he manifests himself and attends to that devotee's care. Lord Gopinath, knowing me to be as lowly as I am, keeps me close to the feet of your servant. Narsinh Mehta says, "I am entangled in maya and am poor, poor," so he says.)

The places and gateways for attaining this liberation-moksha have been named in the mortal world (mrityulok) — the four things named above, their locations are shown here. A verse from the Niranjan Puran:

_sapta puryo trayo grama, navaranya navaushadhah, chaturdashani guhyani mukti-dvara iva vartate ||4||_ (Seven cities, three villages, nine forests, nine medicinal herbs, and fourteen guhyas — all these are gateways to liberation.)

Commentary: The places named for attaining moksha in the mortal world are said to be seven cities, three villages, nine forests, nine medicinal herbs, and fourteen secret (guhya) sites. If one dwells at these places and worships Parbrahm, one attains moksha. But what has been shown here is described as belonging to the mixture of the path of action (karma-marg); therefore this path is not complete, for wherever the path of action, ritual and rites, comes in, the influence of maya increases, and instead of attaining liberation, the soul is left wandering through the universe. This same point is shown in the scriptures — that the texts composed by Brahmins were made to cast the ordinary soul into delusion. Jivanji Maharaj draws attention to exactly this.

In the Vishnu Sahasranama, Vishnu's 542nd name is "Guhya." Shankaracharya wrote of Guhya that it can be known only through the secret knowledge of the Upanishads, or, since guha means "cave," it is called guhya because it lies hidden in the space of the heart. But those who point out these sites on the path of liberation run a hidden system of yoga, and there are said to be fourteen kinds of such guhyas. In continuation of the fourth verse, which showed forty-two sites for attaining liberation, there is a verse in the explanatory commentary on the Bal Kand of Tulsidas's Ramayan:

_saptapuri trayo grama, navaranya navaushara, navaite nagar khyata, ashtau te patna smritah ||10||_ (Commentary: These forty-five, 45, fields are gateways to liberation on earth; among them all the seven cities are foremost, and among those seven, Ayodhya is foremost.) There is, further, a verse in the explanatory commentary on the Uttar Kand:

_sapta pantha pancha kshetra durgam ekona vinshati, chaturdashani guhyani mukti dvarani bhutale ||11|| saptapur trayo gram, navaranya navaushara, navaisi nagara khyata, ashtaite pattan smrita ||12|| saptapantha pancha kshetra durgam ekona vinshati, chaturdashani guhyani mukti-dvarani bhutale ||13||_ (Commentary: Ramchandra told Sugriv, Angad, and Vibhishan that the city of Ayodhya is exceedingly holy. Though Vaikunth is praised, as known in the Vedas and Puranas and known to the whole world, yet to me Vaikunth is not as dear as Ayodhya — Ayodhya is dearer to me than Vaikunth. Seeing this episode, no learned person fails to know that the meaning of "Ayodhya" is "unrivaled" — that is, of all the places on earth, Ayodhya is supreme above all. These fifty-two, bavanu, fields are gateways to liberation on earth; among all of them the seven cities are foremost, and among those seven, Ayodhya too is foremost.)

Six cities, 3 villages, 9 forests, 9 medicinal herbs, 9 towns, 8 ports, 6 paths, 5 fields, 21 forts, 14 guhyas — 92 in total — are the places for attaining liberation named in the mortal world.

The three villages: these three villages are as follows.

In Mahayog — Shaligram.
In Harimandir — Shambhalgram.
In Kaushal Desh — Nandi Gram, Nand Gram.

(Shambhal taluka is 23 miles from Muradabad. The Kalki avatar will be born in the house of the Brahmin Vishnuyash; his mother Sumati will give birth to him on the 12th of the bright half of Vaishakh, Vai. Su. 12. Garud's portion will give him his horse, the all-knowing parrot, and Shiv will give him his sword. He will marry Pannavati, daughter of Brihadrath of Ceylon. Jay and Vijay will be his sons. Kalyan, Year 5, Issue 1, pages 464 to 467, mentions the second village; there Nandigram is said to be one kos from Ayodhya.) Besides these, other villages have also been named as follows:

Rohit Gram — situated on the Kapivati river.
Vinat Gram — a village on the Gomati river.
Jambuprastagram, Toran Gram, Maha Gram, Varuth Gram, Hastiprishthak Gram, and others are also mentioned.

In the last page of the Ayodhya Mahatmya, the three villages, trigram, are described:

_teen gram hai muktike data tinke naam suno jagatrata, shaligram pathik hai gaava doosar naam bimal gun gaava, tisar avdayak hai grama tinoke as kahai nama. — doha — ja teeno yah gaam hai phaldayak hai char, bahu tapasvin yah tap kiya paayo hai sukh saar ||33||_ (O Ram, savior of the world, listen — three villages grant liberation. The first, Shaligram, is walking the path of devotion. The second is singing the pure qualities of the Lord's name. The third is pure conduct, holy action — that is the third village. These are the names of the three. These three villages are the givers of the four attainments; when ascetics perform great austerities, they obtain this blissful attainment.)

The nine forests: 1. Dandak, Dandavan; 2. Saindhavaranya, Siddhiban; 3. Jambumarg, Jambuk; 4. Pushkal, Pushkban; 5. Utpalavart, Ghorvan; 6. Naimishyaranya, Yugalihiban; 7. Kuruban-jangal, Shubhaban; 8. Arbuda, Anbanban; 9. Hemvant, Himban.

Among forests, fourteen forests are also counted: 1. Champakaranya, 2. Badrikaranya, 3. Dandakaranya, 4. Arbudaranya, 5. Dharmaranya, 6. Pashanmaranya, 7. Guhyaranya, 8. Jambukaranya, 9. Vindhyaranya, 10. Drakshaaranya, 11. Nahushaaranya, 12. Kamyakaranya, 13. Dvaitaranya, 14. Naimishyaranya.

Guhya: The Yajurved produced sacrifices through the ritual procedures of yajnas. The difference between yajna and rtu is this: where a sacrificial post (yupa) is built for binding animals, that is called rtu. Then came dakshina, the ritual gift; then the era of samvatsar, the yearly cycle. As the fruit of the yajna-performing patron, the heavenly worlds came into being (svarga and so on); then the gods came into being; then subsidiary deities such as the Guhyakas came into being; then the twelve Sadhyaganas came into being. (Bhagavat Darshan, Vol. 87, p. 57.)

The fourteen places:

_chaudah jo sthan hai, avadhpurike manhi, tako phal bahutai kaho, samjho sab mili tahi ||34||_ (Amar Bharat, Vol. 2, p. 180) (Note No. 1, p. 118) (Regarding the fourteen sites in Avadhpuri, its fruit is said to be very great — so all of you together should understand it.)

Guh: Because Skanda dwelt in a golden vessel for six days before his birth, he was called Guh. Shankaracharya, in one commentary on the 383rd name of Vishnu in the Vishnu Sahasranama, "Guh," said: because he conceals his own true form and so on by his maya — that is, he covers it up — he is called Guh. The Lord's own words:

_naham prakashah sarvasya yogamaya samavritah ||14||_ (Gita 7-25) (Veiled by my yogamaya, I am not manifest to all.)

The ritualist Brahmin school has, in this manner, given foremost status to pilgrimage sites and deities, and counted them as places for attaining liberation. But all these are distractions in the way of devotion to Vishnu. Therefore, whether the sites number fifty-two, bavanu, or ninety-two, banu, the Samagam does not accept them. It counsels one to stay watchful against all these entanglements, warning us not to fall into these temptations. All these are deceptive doings that trick us in the name of moksha.

Guard against craving for liberation.

_kabir mugat na maagun bhagatin chhandun, hari gun sunat sunaau, raam krishn avatar manorath, janam janam gun gaau ||35||_ (Naam Rup) (Baba Kabirji says, "I do not ask for liberation; I ask only this — that I never give up your devotion, that I hear and recite the praises of Hari, and that, holding the wish that you take avatar as Ram and as Krishna, I keep singing your praises birth after birth. This alone I ask.")

_kabir matvala naamka, piyo prem ras aghai, matvala didarka, maage mugat balai ||36||_ (Baba Kabirji says, "I have become utterly intoxicated with the Lord's name; I have drunk deep and full of the nectar of love; I have become drunk with rapture in the vision of the Lord's form. So now, let whatever calamity is upon me ask for liberation — I myself will never, ever ask for liberation.")

Now let us see what the 96 pakhands, sects, are.

"96 Pakhand," Rev. Yadunath, Litiyu 92, p. 53, 55: the pandits of the philosophical schools, darshan shastras, making small and large distinctions, made sixteen divisions, and each darshan came to have six-six divisions — these very divisions are called pakhand.

As described in the Samagam, the 52–92 sites named for attaining moksha belong to the path of action, karma-marg; they belong to the six darshans. Each single darshan has 16 pakhands; thus for all six darshans together there are in total 16 x 16 = 96 pakhands.

Each pakhand has three gachchhas, sub-sects. Among the Jains too there are two divisions, but the scriptures count both as one: (1) Digambar, (2) Shvetambar. Jain — 1, one; Buddhist — 3, three; Charvak — 2, two; these are the names of the three gachchhas. Wherever a particular gachchha exists, that particular pakhand and that particular gachchha are found there.

In Registration No. 541, p. 39, Dharekhan writes that caste (jnati) and gachchha are different things. Caste is not gachchha; gachchha arose from different lineages and branches. Gachchha is called gotra. In all there are 84–85 gachchhas; at present few remain. Inter-dining and inter-marriage do not exist among many of them, though the scriptures do not forbid it. Many have made efforts to separate the Jains from the Hindus. In the Samagam, Kabirji's ramaini is presented as testimony regarding the gayatri and so on of the pakhand-gachchhas.

Shankaracharya has said:

_gajairapi pidyamano'pi na gacchejjainamandire, yavani naiva vaktavya pranaih kanthagatairapi ||15||_

It further says:

_hastina tadyamano'pi na gacchejjainamandiram, na vadedyavanim bhasham pranaih kanthagatairapi ||16||_ (Registration No. 1613, p. 37) (Even if trampled by an elephant, one should not enter a Jain temple to save oneself; and even if life is leaving one through the throat, one should not speak the language of the Yavanas, the Greek/foreign barbarians.)

Now let us speak of the six, shat, darshan shastras. Each of the six darshan shastras has sixteen-sixteen pakhands; for all six darshans together this makes 16 x 6 = 96 pakhands.

Indian philosophical schools, darshan shastras, are divided into two groups: those holding Vedic belief, that is, darshan shastras that accept the Veda, and non-Vedic shastras, that is, those opposed to the Veda. Six darshan shastras favoring the Veda are named:

1) Nyaya Shastra — Gautam Muni
2) Vaisheshik Shastra — Kanad Muni
3) Sankhya Darshan — Kapil Muni
4) Yoga Darshan — Patanjali
5) Purva Mimamsa — Jaimini
6) Uttar Mimamsa — Badarayan

The non-Vedic, or Veda-opposing, darshan shastras are also six:
1) Lokayatik — (unspecified)
2) Charvak Darshan — Charvak Muni
3) Mahayan Darshan — Gautam Buddha
4) Vrajyan Darshan — Gautam Buddha
5) Hinayan Darshan — Gautam Buddha
6) Jain Darshan — Mahavir Swami

96 pakhands, 12 yogis, 18 jangams, 24 sevadas, 10 sannyasis, 14 darvesh (sheikhs), and 18 brahmins.

Thus altogether twelve darshan shastras have been named. Of the first six, two — Sankhya and Purva Mimamsa — are nirishvaravadi, that is, they do not believe in God. Purva Mimamsa upholds ritual action (karmakand): it holds that the Vedic mantras alone bestow all fruits. In their view, man acts only in hope of fruit, and fruit is obtained through Vedic mantras; therefore there is no need for the soul (jiva), the world, or God.

But what Sadguru Shri Jivanji Maharaj says about this doctrine of pakhand is as follows. Among the darshan shastras, whether they accept the Veda or not, there has never been unanimous agreement on matters such as the body, the soul, and God. There prevails dispute, that is, doctrinal disagreement, among all of them. Yet, despite this mutual opposition, an attempt is made to show doctrinal non-contradiction and to bring about reconciliation. According to the Jain view, of the many attributes of a single thing, one attribute is considered primary and the rest secondary — cultivating the outlook of seeing and understanding a thing from different standpoints. Gautam Muni, the founder of Nyaya Shastra, in order to know Brahma, to attain moksha, enumerated sixteen distinct categories:

1) Pramana, means of valid knowledge: The instrument of true knowledge, divided into four: 1) Pratyaksha, perception, 2) Anuman, inference, 3) Upaman, comparison, 4) Shabda, verbal testimony.

2) Prameya, the object of knowledge: That which can become the object of true knowledge. Twelve kinds of prameya are named: soul, body, senses, objects, intellect, mind, activity, rebirth, fault, fruit, suffering, and liberation — knowledge that touches the mutually contradictory aspects present within one and the same subject.

3) Samshaya, doubt: Knowledge that touches upon mutually contradictory aspects of a single object, once a purpose or aim has arisen for it.

4) Prayojana, purpose: That thing for the sake of which an activity is undertaken, whether to attain or to avoid it.

5) Drishtanta, example: That regarding which there is no difference of opinion between the scholar and common practice.

6) Siddhanta, established tenet: This has four kinds — 1) Sarvatantra, universally accepted, 2) Pratitantra, school-specific, 3) Adhikaran, implied by the topic, 4) Abhyupagam, hypothetically granted.

7) Avayava, the members of a syllogism, which are five: 1) Pratijna, proposition, 2) Hetu, reason, 3) Udaharan, example, 4) Upanayan, application, 5) Nigaman, conclusion.

8) Tarka, reasoning: When the true nature of some thing is not known, then, in order to discover its nature, one infers one thing and, on that basis, infers a further, undifferentiated thing.

9) Nirnaya, ascertainment: After doubt has arisen, the determination of one of the two sides through a position (paksha) and a counter-position (pratipaksha).

10) Vada, debate: That verbal exchange in which both a thesis and a counter-thesis are accepted — that is, in which, of the two mutually opposed aspects of a single subject, the proponent and the opponent have each duly accepted one aspect as their own position, in which both proponent and opponent establish their own position and refute the other's through proof and reasoning, in which this process of establishing and refuting takes the form of statements composed of the five members, proposition and so on, and which does not go against established doctrine.

11) Jalpa: In addition to having all the aforesaid characteristics of Vada, that verbal exchange in which deceit (chhala), sophistry (jati), and disqualifying tactics (nigrahasthan) are also employed to establish one's own side and refute the opposing side is called Jalpa.

12) Vitanda: That same Jalpa, if we remove from it the establishing of one's own counter-position, is called Vitanda.

13) Hetvabhasa, fallacious reason: That which, though not a true reason, appears to be a reason. There are five kinds: 1) Savyabhichar, inconclusive, 2) Viruddha, contradictory, 3) Prakaranasam, equal to the point at issue, 4) Sadhyasam, equal to what is to be proved, 5) Badhit, contradicted by other proof.

14) Chhala, deceit: Imagining a meaning different from what a person intended to say, and thereby corrupting that person's statement. Its kinds are Vak-chhala, Samanya-chhala, and Upachar-chhala.

15) Jati, sophistry: Bringing about an undesired consequence through resemblance and non-resemblance, that is, through similarity and dissimilarity.

16) Nigrahasthan, point of defeat: That point at which, owing to self-contradiction or a failure to state one's position, the disputant must be stopped.

(Tarkasangraha, composed by Annambhatta; English translation by Yashwant Vasudev Athavale and Mahadev Rajaram Bodas.)

The soul, the world, Brahma, Parbrahm, and so on cannot be established through scriptural debate — these can be known only through one's own direct experience, self-realization.

On "pakhand," in the Sundarvilas composed by Sundardas, pakhand, hypocrisy and pretense, is enumerated as follows:

1. Some people perform yajnas according to Vedic ritual — Vajapeya, Gomedha, and so on.

2. Some people wander from one pilgrimage site to another.

3. Some people, through purificatory practice at home, perform sandhya, twilight prayers, tarpan, offerings to ancestors, and the six rites, shatkarma.

4. Some people, taking up the varnashram order, observe brahmacharya and become celibate students.

5. Some people, in the householder stage, remain bound day and night to son and wife in various ways.

6. Some people take the vow of vanaprastha and go to the forest together with their wife.

7. Some people, as paramhansa sannyasis, give up their topknot and sacred thread, yet bind themselves in many other bonds.

8. Some people bathe every day, evening, morning, and noon.

9. Some people observe many rules and vows — the chandrayan vrat, fasting, and so on.

10. Some people worship the gods, plucking various leaves and flowers for worship.

11. Some people wear rosaries and tilak and call themselves devotees who worship Vishnu.

12. Some people chant the name of Shiva endlessly, hang a linga around the neck, and smear themselves with ash.

13. Some Jains, upholding the doctrine of karma, have their hair plucked out and perform excessive show.

14. Some people wear earrings and, as Kapalikas, Aghoris, follow a corrupt doctrine.

15. Some people, through fierce atheistic doctrine, commit much pakhand.

16. Some people take the Goddess to be Shakti and kill living creatures to offer to her.

17. Some people perform many kinds of homa — sesame offerings, japa, ghee lamps — and serve her in this way.

18. Some people perform yajna and homa, make offerings to the gods, and serve them with incense and lamps.

19. Some people practice impure mantras, black magic — vashikaran, subjugation, uchchatan, banishing — and perform rites at the cremation pyre.

20. Some people, in cremation grounds, awaken the dead and practice much stambhan, paralyzing, and mohan, bewitching.

21. Some people attract women and cheat them, stealing away their ornaments.

22. Some people, spreading falsehoods, transmute metals through the alchemy of mercury into gold.

23. Some people make wonder-working pills from plant leaves and gain occult powers.

24. Some people hold sharp-edged swords, fire, and water under their control, and lift boulders onto their shoulders.

25. Some people improve bodily health through medicinal herbs and roots.

26. Some people, through astrological calculation, run household affairs by determining the date, day, hour, and auspicious moment.

27. Some people give in charity by weighing themselves against gold, tuladan, and give gems, land, grain, cloth, books, and other various gifts.

28. Some people speak Sanskrit, know difficult verses, and recite them to others.

29. Some people study logic, tarkashastra, and, having mastered this learning, carry a staff as a badge of authority.

30. Some people know various differing doctrines and display cleverness by studying grammar.

31. Some people recite poetry and verse, composing kundaliyas and other such forms.

32. They string together verses and stanzas, stealing syllables from wherever they can.

33. They play the veena and flute, singing songs to the beat of drums.

34. Some people display the art of actors, singing sweetly with hand gestures.

35. Some people undergo severe bodily austerities and eat only a handful of food, panchagrasa.

36. Some people eat as if with an elephant's mouth, excessively, and then fall on their knees, gaining no wisdom at all.

37. Some people stretch out their hand to beg alms, and then, wiping their hand, run off into the forest.

38. Some people go from door to door begging for stale, dry scraps of bread.

39. Some people cook without touching anyone, and display this to people with their mouths covered.

40. Some people eat morsels served by a woman's hand from an iron plate.

41. Some people wash their food and drink the washings, living in such filth that one wonders how they survive at all.

42. Some people take up the doctrine of the Aghoris, accepting both extremes.

43. Some people eat forbidden food without fear, even eating meat and drinking liquor.

44. Some poor people live only on milk, payahari, eating raisins, dried coconut, grapes, and dates.

45. Some people dig up and eat roots and tubers, living alone in the forest.

46. Some people wear tree bark and sit in deep water reciting japa.

47. Some people dye their clothes yellow and wear very thin garments.

48. Some people, appearing steeped in devotion and free of passion, wear torn saffron robes.

49. Some deceitful people wear rough, prickly wooden garments, making a great show and shouting loudly while sitting in deep water reciting japa.

50. Some people wear clothes of coarse sackcloth to please and win over people in many ways.

51. Some people pick up rags from the road and, carrying a beggar's bag, present themselves in the guise of the formless, nirgun.

52. Some people wear deerskin or tiger skin, putting on great pretense and show.

53. Some people wear bark garments and endure cold and rain.

54. Some people go about naked, as digambaras, and smear themselves with ash.

55. Some people grow matted hair and long nails; the Lord does not recognize such varied forms.

56. Some people test their ignorance and, being dull-witted, burn in the heat of the five fires, panchagni.

57. Some people sit amid thunder and, in cold weather, enter into water.

58. Some people, smoking and losing their way, hang upside down from trees.

59. Some fools die by the sword's edge in their desire to become kings.

60. Some people, for the sake of happiness in the next birth, jump from a height into water and die.

61. Some fools waste their bones away in the Himalayas, their minds greatly pleased at doing so.

62. Some people pierce their throat and give up the body, hoping to gain something in the life to come.

63. Some people dwell on mountains, and some dwell in caves.

64. Some people do not stay in one place — today here, tomorrow they go elsewhere.

65. Some people make their bed of grass.

66. Some people spread hard pebbles for their bed.

67. Some people observe harsh vows, standing on one leg for twelve years.

68. Some people go and live in cremation grounds, proudly claiming, "I am an avadhut."

69. Some people live beneath trees, saying, "I depend on no one."

70. Some people keep silent and do not speak, communicating their inner thoughts through gestures.

71. Some people shave sandalwood into sandals and, wearing sandals on their feet, wink their eyes.

72. Some people act as swindlers, robbing everyone in plain sight.

73. Some people smear vermilion on their bodies and keep a child with them.

74. Some people cast spells, mooth, saying, "May Narsimha and Bhairav strike you down."

75. Some people eat akdo and dhaturo, poisonous plants, and put burning coals into their mouths.

76. Some people eat opium and drink bhang, being dull-minded and whimsical.

77. How far should one go on counting such wanderers? Understanding this, one should remain in the shelter of the Guru.

The King of Riva has enumerated the 96 pakhands as follows:

_dash sanyasi barah yogi, chaudah shekh bakhana, bodh adharahi jangam adharahi, chaubees savera jana ||37||_ (In this way the 96 pakhands are told. Kabir Ramaini Sudha, page 4, writes: ten kinds of sannyasis, twelve kinds of yogis, eighteen kinds of brahmins, eighteen kinds of other castes — Shia-Sunni, Christian, Parsi, and so on — fourteen kinds of Sheikhs, and twenty-four kinds of Jains — in total, ninety-six, 96, kinds. All these divisions were created by man himself; the Supreme is not responsible for them.)

It further says:

_yogi jangam sevda, sanyasi daravesh, chhatha kahiye brahmanan, chha ghar chha updesh ||38||_ (These six darshans have six mantra-teachings.)

1. Jogi — "Ahannad"; 2. Jangam — "Niranjanay"; 3. Sevda — "Arihant"; 4. Brahmin — "Ukar," the Gayatri's Omkar; 5. Darvesh — "I am Allah"; 6. Sannyasi — "Soham, Brahmasmi."

Jogi: those who have performed the practice of "ear-slit," kanphata, yoga, such as Matsyendra and others.
Jangam: those who tie the linga of Mahadev around their neck and live together with a woman.
Sevda: followers of the Jain doctrine — the Sthanakvasi and the temple-dwelling, Deravasi, Jains.
Sannyasi: those who wear saffron robes and bear one of the ten names, dashnam — Giri, Puri, Bharati, Van, Parvat, Sagar, Tirth, Parvat, Dungar, Jhadvan, and so on — this is the darshan of the sannyasi.
Darvesh: Muslim fakirs, auliya, and so on.
Brahmin: ritualists, karmakandi. Among these six darshans there are ninety-six pakhands.

The six divisions of the atheistic, nastik, schools outside the Veda are: 1. Vaibhashik, 2. Saubhantik, 3. Yogachar, 4. Madhyamik, 5. Jain — Digambar, 6. Charvak.

Regarding those who don religious garb, the Panchatantra, in the Kakolukiyam chapter, verse 98, says:

_nacchadayati kaupinam na damshamashakapaham, shunah puchchhamiva vyartham panditam dharmavarjitam ||17||_ (Just as a dog's tail neither covers its private parts nor drives away flies and mosquitoes, so too is dharma-less scriptural cleverness, which produces no true renunciation, like a dog's tail — useless. Such a person, wearing the loincloth, becoming a sannyasi, is unable to destroy mental afflictions such as lust, and is therefore a failure.)

There is a verse regarding the six scriptures of the six darshans:

_vedant tark mimansa sankhya patanjalam tatha, dharmashastrametyetat prahuh shastranishad budhah ||18||_ (Vedanta, Tarka, Nyaya, Mimansa, Sankhya, Patanjal Yoga, and Dharmashastra — the wise say these are the six shastras.)

For the six darshans it is said: 1. Upanishad, 2. Nyaya, 3. Karmakand, Mimansa, 4. Tattva-vivechan, Sankhya, 5. Yoga, and 6. Smritis. In the Samagam, the six darshans have been divided according to the three gunas, as follows:

1. Sattvik — two darshans of Vishnu's guna: 1. Mahatma = Jogi, 2. Yati = Sevda.
2. Tamasik — 1. Jangam, Lingayat, 2. Sannyasi.
3. Rajasi — 1. Brahmin, 2. Sufi, Darvesh.

The Samagam explains that among those who follow these six darshans, neither the tilak, nor the tulsi, nor the name of Ram is given credence. And the darshan of Vasudev — that is, of devotion to God, the devotion of the true Vaishnav, the devotee of God — stands beyond these six darshans. But people of the world count the devotion of the Vaishnav among the six darshans; yet it remains excluded from them — that devotion is separate from the six darshans. Six scriptures of the six darshans have been composed, but this devotion to Vishnu is different from those six scriptures. The Samagam states that within these true scriptures there is one portion in which devotion to Vishnu is also accepted, and another portion that favors ritual action, karmakand. Thus, of the fourteen kands of the Yajurved, up to the thirteen-and-a-half, 13½, kand there is a mixture of devotion and liberation, through which the soul cannot attain the Supreme. Therefore, having considered all these ritualistic scriptures and the six darshans, one should set them aside — that is, not fall into them — and reject them.

That ritual action is described up to the thirteen-and-a-half kand of the Yajurved is something Kabirji too has pointed out. Regarding the fact that the thirteen-and-a-half kands of the Yajurved uphold ritual action, Kabir has said:

_kabir ter bhag trigun lagi, chauda chotha manhe, e padku je paavhi, ant kahu nahi jaahe ||39||_ (Kabirji says that the thirteen, thirteen-and-a-half, parts of the ritual action, of the Yajurved and so on, can lead only up to the stage of the three gunas, whereas the remaining half of the fourteenth part carries one beyond the three gunas, to the fourth state, the state transcending the three gunas, trigunatita. Therefore, whoever attains this state of the fourth guna will, in the end, no longer have to suffer the pains of birth and death.)

In the mortal world, those on the path of action have designated the seven cities, three villages, nine forests, nine medicinal herbs, fourteen guhyas, and so on as centers for attaining liberation. Among these, again, the seven cities are singled out separately. Rev. Yadunath Maharaj says that even the Smritis, which set forth the ritual action of the six darshans, are to be considered artificial — souls remain caught wandering, as if between a gourd-vessel, between sky and earth. Among the sites for attaining moksha, the seven cities are singled out, and this is given in the Garud Puran, Chapter 16, verse 114:

_ayodhya mathura maya kashi kanchi avantika |_
